title: Grain refinement of self-supported copper electrode by multiple-redox treatment for enhanced carbon dioxide electroreduction towards carbon monoxide generation
abstract: Inspired by grain refinement in the traditional metal processing, we develop a top-down approach by facile multiple-redox treatment to obtain the downsized Cu crystals over the self-supported copper electrodes for the enhanced selective CO2 electroreduction. Specifically, the treated copper meshes exhibit an increased activity and selectivity for CO production with high Faradaic efficiency of 78% and partial current density of 13.2 mA cm 2 at the potential of 0.8 V (vs. RHE). This investigation intends to ascribe the enhanced properties to the surface downsized crystals of Cu electrode induced by the multiple-redox treatments. Moreover, the molecular reaction mechanism of the elementary reaction of CO2 conversion to CO is also discussed. This work offers a new top-down strategy to design and preparation of nanosized catalytic catalysts on a self-supported electrode and valuable insights in selective CO2 conversion toward valuable fuels over Cu-based electrodes. 2019 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

a b s t r a c t
Inspired by grain refinement in the traditional metal processing, we develop a top-down approach by facile multiple-redox treatment to obtain the downsized Cu crystals over the self-supported copper electrodes for the enhanced selective CO2 electroreduction. Specifically, the treated copper meshes exhibit an increased activity and selectivity for CO production with high Faradaic efficiency of 78% and partial current density of 13.2 mA cm 2 at the potential of 0.8 V (vs. RHE). This investigation intends to ascribe the enhanced properties to the surface downsized crystals of Cu electrode induced by the multiple-redox treatments. Moreover, the molecular reaction mechanism of the elementary reaction of CO2 conversion to CO is also discussed. This work offers a new top-down strategy to design and preparation of nanosized catalytic catalysts on a self-supported electrode and valuable insights in selective CO2 conversion toward valuable fuels over Cu-based electrodes.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
In the preceding decades, the massive carbon dioxide (CO2) emission into the atmosphere has triggered extreme climate and environmental problems, for instance, global warming and ocean acidification [1]. Consequently, the cutting-edge technologies for CO2 capture, storage, and conversion are becoming more and more exigent for the sustainable development of environment and human society [2]. Electrochemical CO2 reduction is reflected as an auspicious way out due to the well-regulated process for producing valuable chemicals and fuels at moderate conditions [3,4]. Bearing in mind the exceptionally stable C@O bond, efficient electrocatalyst is essential to accelerate the sluggish reaction kinetics of CO2 reduction for desirable product generation [5–9]. Due to the abundant reduction products with high total products efficiency, copper (Cu)-based materials are eye-catching among the various electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction [10].
Generally, CO2 reduction over Cu-based materials produces a wide range of gas and liquid products, such as hydrocarbon, formic
acid, alcohol and carbon monoxide (CO) [10,11]. Among them, CO is an essential rawmaterial for organic chemistry and C1 chemistry in modern industry. Various strategies including tuning crystal structure (size/defect/twin/grain boundary) [12,13] and composition (alloying) have been developed to construct nanocatalysts for the enhanced CO production through the CO2 electroreduction [14–16]. More importantly, the CO2 electroreduction process always goes along with hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) on metallic materials, which results in a poor activity and selectivity for the CO production [17–20]. Synthesis of nanosized Cu-based catalyst is recognized as one of the most effective ways for catalytic CO2 electrolysis [21–26]. Advanced progress has been achieved afterward by the bottom-up method to construct the delicate nanoparticles, but the poor catalytic activity and product selectivity is still the bottleneck for Cu-based composites in the electrochemical CO2 conversion towards CO production [27,28]. Moreover, it is still far from the satisfaction for the CO production because of the elaborate bottom-up strategy and complicated synthesis procedure, as these as-obtained Cu nanocatalysts will be remixed with organic binders and sprayed on supporting materials to assemble the gas diffusion electrode (GDE). This process would complicate the fabrication of these Cu nanocatalysts integrated membrane electrode assemblies (MEA) and their subsequent
application in the practical CO2 electrolysis flow cells [29]. Furthermore, the mechanism understanding while involving the performance with the structural feature is still questioned. Some researchers regard the residual or subsurface oxygen as active sites [24,30], while others claim the metallic Cu nanostructure as the origin of catalytic activity [31,32]. For this purpose, developing an effective top-down strategy to directly fabricate the selfsupported binder-free electrodes integrated with Cu electrocatalyst may be desirable and of capital significance for the practical CO2 conversion towards highly selective CO production [33–38].
Inspired by the grain refinement behaviors in the traditional metal processing, herein we report a simple top-down strategy by the multiple-redox method to fabricate the self-supported binder-free Cu electrodes for selective CO2 electroreduction towards CO production. As expected, these self-supported Cu meshes demonstrate the down-sized Cu nanocrystals with abundant grain boundary and enhanced surface area along with the increased redox cycles. Notably, a significantly improved selectivity of CO formation as well as the activity of CO2 electroreduction is achieved. The Faradaic efficiency (FE) of CO production is significantly increased from ~5.0% for the initial Cu mesh to ~78% for the multiple-redox treated Cu mesh at the potential of 0.8 V (vs. RHE). Such improvement is attributed to the enhanced surface chemistry rather than the simple inhibition of HER, as the partial current densities of CO product is also significantly increased from 0.03 mA cm 2 to 13.2 mA cm 2 over the self-supported Cu electrode. Also, based on the molecular reaction mechanism for CO2 conversion to CO, the self-supported Cu electrode with downsized nanocrystals obtained by the multiple-redox treatment might be favorable to every elementary reaction. This work not only reports an effective top-down approach to realize the grain refinement and fabricate the self-supported Cu electrodes but more significantly offers valuable insights in understanding the enhancement mechanism of Cu electrodes for selective and effective CO2 conversion towards CO production.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Cu mesh (200 200 mesh, thickness: 0.1 cm), KHCO3 (99%, AR), HClO4 (70%wt, AR) and KOH (95%, AR) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. High purity argon gas (99.9999%) and carbon dioxide (99.999%) were purchased from Huaerwen Gas Ltd.

sections.heading: 2.2. Preparation
sections.text: The Cu mesh (1 cm 2 cm 0.1 cm, 200 200 mesh) substrates (denoted as Cu-0) were alternately washed with deionized water (18.2 MX) and acetone for three times. They were then sonicated in 0.1 M HClO4 solution for 20 s followed by repeatedly rinsing with deionized water. After drying under Ar atmosphere, this Cu mesh substrate was placed in a quartz boat preset to 500 C (5 C min 1) and annealed in the air for 4 h in a box furnace. Then, the synthesized Cu oxides (denoted as Cu-OX) substrates were electrochemically reduced in 0.1 M KHCO3 at 1.0 V (vs. RHE) until the substrates surface begun to produce bubbles. After the reduction process, the Cu electrode was washed with deionized water three times and then transferred to another H-type cell with the fresh 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. The fresh solution was used for each electroreduction treatment and measurement. The obtained Cu substrates (Cu-X) and initial Cu mesh (Cu-0) were then used as electrodes for electrochemical catalytic studies.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization
sections.text: All samples were prepared for scanning transmission electron microscopy (SEM) examination on a Nova Nano SEM 450 field emission scanning electron microscope. Wide-angle X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on an X’pert3 powder diffractometer operating at 40 mA and 40 kV equipped with a Cu Ka source (k = 0.1540598). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) studies were performed on an ESCALAB 250 Xi with Al Ka (hk = 1 486.6 eV) as the excitation source, and the vacuum degree of analysis room was set as 10 10 Pa. The binding energies obtained in the XPS spectral analysis were calibrated by C1s = 284.8 eV. TEM images and high-resolution TEM images were obtained by JEOL JEM-2100 with an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. For TEM observation, the sample was prepared by 5 h ultrasound.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurement
sections.text:
A standard three-electrode airtight electrochemical H-type cell configuration with two compartments was used for all tests. The anode and cathode compartments were separated with a proton exchange membrane (Nafion 117, Dupont). As the working electrode, the reverse side of Cu electrode was encapsulated with polyamide tape to normalize the current. Platinum gauze electrode and Ag/AgCl electrode were used as counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. Before the CO2 reduction measurements, CO2 was bubbled into the 0.1 M KHCO3 for at least 30 min under magnetically stirring (pH = 6.8, potentials are concerning the reverse hydrogen electrode (RHE), E(RHE) = E(Ag/AgCl) + 0.6 V). All electrochemical experiments were performed on a computercontrolled CHI 760E electrochemical workstation. For the whole reduction reaction, gaseous products were detected by both online Shimadzu gas chromatography (GC-2014) and Panna GC (A91) systems. Also, the reduction experiments from Cu-OX to CuX at the potential of 0.8 V through chronoamperometry in 0.1 M KHCO3 were cut off until the mesh substrate starts to bubble, at that moment, the primary reaction of electrolysis was HER due to the Cu-OX was reduced completely. CO electro-oxidation was also conducted in an airtight electrochemical H-type cell. Before the electrooxidation, the catalyst was cycled in the Ar-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte until a well-established cyclic voltammogram was observed. Then, CO was bubbled into the electrolyte and forming a saturated CO adlayer by holding at 0.05 V (vs. RHE) for 10 min. After that, the electrolyte was again purged with Ar to remove needless CO, thus the CO monolayer electrooxidation curves were recorded in CO-free on the potential window of 0.1 V ~ 1.1 V at a scan rate of 20 mV s 1. Through 4 h calcining at 500 C on Cu-0 and Cu-X in a tube furnace, the variable mass ratio was detected by weighting their increment of oxides versus Cu-0 and Cu-X. The higher ratio indicates that multiple treatments are more likely to be activated Cu meshes and enable more active sites to expose on the surface of the mesh substrates. Considering roughness factor (Rf) is crucial for electrocatalysts, we compare the roughness factors (Rf) for Cu-0, Cu-1, Cu-2, Cu-3, Cu-4 and Cu-5 mesh electrodes based on the equation: Rf = Cdl/CS, in which Cdl stands for double layer capacitance, while CS stands for the average double-layer capacitance of a smooth metal surface. The Cdl was determined by measuring the capacitive current associated with double-layer charging from the scan-rate dependence of cyclic voltammetric stripping. It can be seen from the formula that the roughness is proportional to the Cdl. The Cdl of Cu-0, Cu-1, Cu-2, Cu-3, Cu-4 and Cu-5 are 1.14, 27.76, 38.22, 47.34, 60.31, and 85.95 mF cm 2, respectively. Assuming the roughness of Cu-0 to be 1, the roughness factors for Cu-1, Cu-2, Cu-3, Cu-4 and Cu-5 mesh electrodes are 24.35, 33.53, 41.52, 52.9 and 78.9, respectively. Moreover, the ECSAs of the samples are calculated based
on the equation: ECSA = Rf S, in which Rf represents roughness factor, S stands for the real surface area of the smooth metal electrode, which was generally equal to the geometric area of Cu mesh (1 cm2). The value of ECSAs for Cu-0, Cu-1, Cu-2, Cu-3, Cu-4 and Cu-5 are 1, 24.35, 33.53, 41.52, 52.9 and 78.9 cm2, respectively.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images show the initial Cu mesh (denoted Cu-0) is composed of Cu fibers with a smooth surface (Fig. S1). The different Cu meshes treated by the oxidation and electroreduction are denoted as Cu-OX and Cu-X (X = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), respectively, according to the cycle number (X) of redox treatments. After the first oxidation treatment, the smooth surface is destroyed and the dense and aligned nanowires of 100–400 nm in diameter and 4–10 lm in length appear on the surface of Cu mesh. Meanwhile, many raised and uplifted oxides grains are also observed at the undersurface of Cu-O1 (Fig. S2a-c). After the first electrochemical reduction at 1.0 V, the as-obtained Cu-1 mesh is deformed in some degree, the wrinkles overspread the nanowires, and the particles are emerged on the surface (Fig. S2d-f). Notably, the subsurface morphology demonstrates a porous structure, which would be ascribed to the deoxygenate process. In the second redox cycle, most of the nanowires fall off the Cu mesh (Fig. S3a). The fracture cross-section analysis of the residual nanowires root indicates that the pulverization of nanowires is induced by the strain produced in the re-oxidation process (Fig. S3b). With the increased redox cycles, the crystallized undersurface turns to be smooth hillocky oxides particles after each oxidation process, while the following electroreduction processes could break the hillocky oxides into cracked blocks with particle refinement (Fig. S36). After 5 times redox treatments, the as-obtained Cu-5 mesh shows a porous surface with the dense and intensive nanoparticle distributed homogeneously (Fig. 1e). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations show that these nanoparticles with an average diameter of 10–15 nm assemble into a rougher and porous surface (Figs. 1f and S7), which is distinguished with the flat surface of initial Cu mesh. During in the multiple-redox treatments of Cu meshes, the oxygenating and deoxygenating process would induce the repeated expansion/contraction and consequently result in the surface roughening and grain refinement, which is common in the traditional metaling and processing of metalcomposites. Therefore, the tiny Cu nanocrystals with abundant grain boundary and enhanced surface area are obtained in the self-supported Cu electrode.
The particle evolution of redox-treated Cu meshes is also supported by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) results. All the Cu-OX samples are dominated by Cu oxides, including Cu2O and CuO phases (Fig. 2a), while the Cu-X samples are verified to be mainly metallic Cu (Fig. 2b). Moreover, the gradual broadening of diffraction peaks for Cu-OX and Cu-X samples through multiple-redox treatments indicates the grain refinement in these Cu meshes (Table S1), where Cu-5 shows a decreased grain size of ~12 nm according to the XRD results. This phenomenon is in accordance with the observation in SEM and TEM images (Fig. 1). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is further employed to characterize the surface composition of Cu-X meshes. Although it is difficult to distinguish the chemical state of Cu (0) and Cu (I) as the overlapped Cu 2p3/2 peaks, the more significant chemical shifts can be observed at Auger peak Cu LMM (auger electron spectroscopy) compared to Cu 2p (Fig. S8) [39]. The main peaks suggest the coexistence of Cu(0) and Cu(I) in Cu-5 at 918.6 eV and 916.7 eV (Fig. 2c). Cu2O still exists in Cu-5, which is likely to be a result of the inevasible exposure of the samples to air (Fig. S9). XPS and XRD results indicate the reduction of CuO and Cu2O in to Cu(0) in the CO2 electroreduction.
Meanwhile, the intensity of Cu(I) peaks at 918.6 eV for Cu-5 is much higher than that of Cu-1 (Fig. S10), which signifies Cu-5 can be quickly suffered from oxidation. On the other hand, the overall peak intensity of Cu 2p and Cu LMM declines gradually spread to the multiple redox processes for Cu-2, Cu-3 Cu-4, and Cu-5 (Figs. 2d and S8). Compared to the nanowires on Cu-1 surface and particles on the subsurface, the Cu-2 mesh demonstrates a porous surface with the dense and intensive nanoparticle. The overall peak intensities of Cu 2p and Cu LMM in Cu-1 mesh is supposed to be weaker than that of Cu-2 according to the surfacesensitive XPS measurement. Hence, the multiple-redox treatment could help to refine the surface grain of the self-supported of Cu mesh, generating more activated Cu sites, which in turn affects their CO2 electroreduction properties for the practical CO2 electrolysis.
The electrocatalytic activity of CO2 reduction over different Cu mesh electrodes are investigated in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 by an H-type cell integrated with both online gas chromatography (GC) systems. As seen in the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements (Figs. 3a and S11), the catalytic activity of CO2 reduction over different Cu electrodes is increased along with the increased number of redox treatments, suggesting the effective redox treatment on the catalyst design. Specifically, the Cu-5 mesh demonstrates the best catalytic performance among five different Cu mesh electrodes (Fig. 3b). Considering metallic Cu compounds are good at the cathodic HER, which is a competitive reaction to CO2 reduction, the step-potential electrolysis coupled with online GC system is employed to analyze the dominating product for several Cu mesh electrodes. Except for trace amount of HCOOH (Fig. S12) and hydrocarbons (CH4 and C2H4, Fig. S13), the gaseous products catalyzed by Cu-X meshes are demonstrated as CO and H2 (Figs. 3c and S14-15). As expected, the initial Cu mesh (Cu-0) shows the dominant hydrogen product with a FE over 95% even at all potential range, while the Cu-5 mesh demonstrates the dominate CO product and presents the highest CO Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 78% at the potential of 0.8 V among all Cu meshes (Fig. 3b). Compared with the previously reported Cu- even Au- or Ag-based catalysts, this multiple-redox treated Cu mesh electrode shows a highly competitive selectivity and activity of CO production in the CO2 conversion (Table S2) [40]. In addition, the redoxtreated Cu-4 and Cu-5 mesh electrodes demonstrate a similar onset potential of 0.2 V vs. RHE (Figs. 3c and S15e), corresponding to an exceptionally low overpotential of only 90 mV, which is much more positive than that of the initial Cu-0 mesh electrode (Fig. S15a). Fig. 3b shows the inhibited side HER and gradually enhanced activity trend of CO2 reduction on Cu mesh electrodes along with the increased redox-treated cycles. These results confirm again that the multiple-redox treatment would not only effectively inhibit HER but also improve CO2 reduction performance over the treated Cu mesh electrodes. Furthermore, the durability of the CO2 electrolysis assembled by Cu-5 mesh electrode is also performed. As illustrated in Fig. 3d, the current density of ~15 mA cm 2 is almost unchanged during the 5 h continuous electrolysis testing. Moreover, the online GC measurements also suggest the stable CO2 electrolysis to CO with a steady FE of over 70%, suggesting the highly active and robust nature of selfsupported Cu mesh electrode for CO2 reduction.
The activity improvement of CO2 conversion to CO on the quantic-redox treated Cu-5 mesh electrode is not just determined by hampering the side hydrogen evolution, as the partial current densities of CO products are also remarkably increased with the redox treatment. Combined LSV curves with FE results, the CO partial current density of Cu-5 mesh is 13.2 mA cm 2 at 0.8 V, which is 37.7, 15.1, 3.9, 2.1 and 1.3 times higher than that of Cu-0, Cu-1, Cu-2, Cu-3 and Cu-4 mesh electrodes (Fig. S16), respectively. Moreover, we compared the kinetics rate-determining step of CO2
reduction by the electrochemical active surface areas (ECSA) corrected current density and Tafel slopes for these six Cu electrodes. The slope close to ~118 mV dec 1 is consistent with a ratedetermining initial electron transfer to CO2 to form a surface adsorbed CO2–* intermediate, which is commonly invoked for metal electrodes.[22,41] A smaller Tafel slope of 121 mV dec 1 for Cu-5 mesh is observed among six Cu electrodes (Fig. 4a), suggesting that the fastest reaction rate for CO2 reduction on Cu-5 electrode could
be triggered by increasing overpotential. The electroreduction of CO2 to CO involves four elementary reaction steps, as shown in the following equations (1–4): CO2 + e +* ? CO2–* (1); CO2–* + H+ ? COOH* (2); COOH*+ H+ + e + ? CO* + H2O (3); CO* ? CO + * (4), where the asterisk (*) indicates a catalytic active site.5, 11 In the first step, an electron is transferred to a CO2 molecule absorbed on the catalytic active site and forms a CO2–* intermediate. The smaller Tafel slope of Cu-5 electrode already suggests a favorable
step (1). Consequently, Cu-5 electrode can efficiently stabilize the CO2–* intermediate and promote the next intermediate reaction. In the following steps (2) and (3), the CO2–* intermediate takes two protons and another electron and forms a CO* intermediate and a H2O molecule. Accordingly, the adsorption of OH– as a substitution for CO2–* is conducted by the oxidative LSV scans to certify the binding affinity of CO2–* on the all Cu electrode samples [42]. Specifically, the overpotential of hydroxyl adsorption is considered as an indicator for the binding strength of intermediates on multiple redox Cu. The smallest overpotential of Cu-5 electrode indicates the stronger adsorption affinity of OH– [27], which implies Cu-5 electrode has a strong binding affinity of CO2–* intermediate (Fig. 4b). Refer to steps (1) and (3), steps (2) and (3) involve a process of intermediate hydrogenation. The proton adsorption and H2 desorption experiments also show the multiple-redox treated Cu electrode can absorb more protons while still desorb less H2 in consideration of current density (Fig. S17). The step (4) only involves the desorption of CO. And all Cu mesh electrode are confirmed by a similar and extremely small electrooxidation peak of CO (Fig. S18). Such a weak electrooxidation peak for CO suggests the weak CO binding strength and easy CO desorption on Cu-X electrodes [43,44].
The enhanced intrinsic activity is related to the grain refinement of Cu nanocrystals induced by the multiple-redox treatments, as the ECSA normalized partial current density for CO production results verified the enhanced FE and partial current density (Fig. 4c). Grain refinement is a normal phenomenon of material deformation in the traditional metal processing. The oxygenating and deoxygenating process in the redox treatment would repeatedly bring the expansion/contraction, this process will consequently produce and release strain, which would induce the grain refining and finally achieve refined grains (Fig. S19). The higher degree of grain refinement will lead to a smaller grain size. With the decrease in grain size, the specific surface area of the electrode will increase swiftly. Based on the results of SEM, XRD and XPS characterization, multiple redox steps did make the surface grain of Cu mesh refine and produced the abundant grain boundaries/defects, thus resulted in the enhanced catalytic active sites. Thus, the catalytic activity of redox Cu is predominately related to the redox cycles, as illustrated in Fig. 3b. The maximal FE of CO of Cu-0 ( 1.1 V), Cu-1 ( 0.4 V), Cu-2 ( 0.7 V), Cu-3 ( 0.7 V), Cu-4 ( 0.8 V) and Cu-5 ( 0.8 V) are 5.5%, 19%, 43%, 68% and 72%, 78%, respectively, which is a positive correlation between the redox cycle and the FEs of CO production. Moreover, the selectivity of CO is in connection with the surface state rather than nanowires (Fig. S20), which is apart from the previous nanowire reports for CO2 electrolysis [16–19]. Additionally, steps (1) and (3) involve one-electron transfer to the solid-liquid interface from the electrode. The charge transfer resistance (Rct) is correlated to the electrons transfer from the catalytic active sites to the reactant [45]. Revealed by the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), a lower Rct of Cu-5 than that of Cu-0 and other Cu-X meshes implies the enhanced charge transfer capability (Fig. S21). The number of active sites is also important to the catalyst performance, and ECSA measurement is thus determined by cyclic voltammetry (CV) in the non-faradaic region (Fig. S22). The higher double layer capacitance (Cdl) is considered to supply larger ECSA with more catalytic active sites (Fig. 4d) [46]. Cu-5 mesh electrode exhibits a remarkably larger ECSA of 89.95 mF cm 2 as compared to Cu-1–4 and Cu-0 counterparts. Specifically, the ECSA of Cu-5 is 75.4-fold higher than that of untreated Cu-0, whereas the Cu-1 electrode is only 24.4 fold. Even after the long-term CO2 electrolysis, Cu-5 electrode still demonstrates the similar surface structure and the remained Cdl value of 80.9 mF cm 2 to the initial 89.95 mF cm 2 (Fig. S23), which shows a good stability and robustness of the Cu-5 electrode (Fig. S24). Throughout the whole electrocatalysis,
catalytic active sites are essential for multi-step CO2 reduction. Moreover, the oxygenation/deoxygenation would promote the formation of tiny crystals and porous structure. This structure would contribute to the enhanced electrochemical surface area and the surface/interface contact for the reactant and products. Therefore, the synergistic effect induced by this facile multiple-redox treatment is responsible for this excellent CO2 reduction to CO over Cu-5 electrode, and this top-down method would provide an effective strategy in design and preparation of self-supported Cu electrodes for practical CO2 electrolysis.
In summary, we report a simple top-down strategy by the multiple-redox method to realize the nanocrystal refinement on the self-supported Cu meshes for selective CO2 electroreduction towards CO production. The treated copper meshes exhibit an increased activity and selectivity for CO2 electroreduction towards CO with a maximum Faradaic efficiency of 78% and high partial current density of 13.2 mA cm 2 at potential of 0.8 V (vs. RHE). We intend to ascribe the enhanced catalytic activity of selfsupported Cu electrode to the surface refinement effect induced by multiple-redox treatments. Our work not only develops a practical top-down approach to realize the surface grain refinement for self-supported Cu electrodes but more significantly offers valuable insights in exploring efficient catalysts and understanding the enhancement mechanism of Cu electrodes for selective and effective CO2 conversion.
